10124-aunt-jane-s-nieces-and-uncle-john:
Edith Van Dyne, writing under that pen name, published this girls' adventure novel in 1911. It brings back Patsy, Beth, and Louise, the nieces of the first books, with their kind, rich Uncle John. When worry over Patsy sparks a plan, the party sets out on a motor tour that soon turns into much more.

A small dog called Mumbles, a wonder on wheels, a fast chauffeur, and stops among Native peoples fill the road west. Capture, escape, a fiddler, and a confession add danger and romance to the fun. Readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned tale of friendship, travel, and pluck.
1110-king-john:
King John of England fights France, quarrels with the Pope, and loses his nephew Arthur, whose death stains his reign. William Shakespeare's history play follows John's troubled rule through battles, truces, and betrayals, with the Bastard Philip Faulconbridge as its witty, loyal heart.

John's crown rests on a shaky claim, and his barons drift toward the French prince. The play ends with John's death and his young son Henry's accession. Its verse is early and vigorous, and the Bastard's speeches give it lasting life on stage. The Bastard's wit and John's fall give the play its lasting stage life.
1511-king-john:
Shakespeare's King John follows the troubled reign of John of England, from a room of state at Northampton to the walls of Angiers in France. Bastard Philip Faulconbridge, John's witty kinsman, steals scenes, while Arthur, the young rival prince, becomes a pawn of French and English crowns.

Through sieges, a papal legate, and a king's death by poison, the play weighs legitimacy, loyalty, and the fate of children in adult wars. Its verse is uneven but its best speeches shine. King John is a lesser-known history, rewarding for readers who love Shakespeare's political mind.
18631-the-lady-of-fort-st-john:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published this historical novel at Boston and New York in 1891 with Houghton, Mifflin and Company. It tells the tragedy of Marie de la Tour at Fort St. John, in what is now New Brunswick. Catherwood, sitting on the height above St. John, says the tale recalls Walter Scott, with reality stranger than fiction.

The story rests on papers about the rival chiefs D'Aulnay and La Tour, two well-born, well-off men whose fights shaped Acadia, then a land covering Nova Scotia and much of Maine. Louis XIII's letter to his governor D'Aulnay shows France meddling from afar. The novel brings early colonial strife to life.
2249-king-john:
John, king of England, faces rebellion at home and war with France over the rival claim of young Arthur. King John moves through sieges, papal excommunication, and shifting alliances as nobles change sides and mothers plead for sons. Shakespeare draws on chronicle history to stage a reign defined by insecure power.

The Bastard Philip Faulconbridge, witty and loyal, emerges as the play's moral center amid the maneuvering. Arthur's fall and John's poisoning close a grim story of ambition without glory. Less famous than the later histories, the play still offers stirring speeches and a bleak view of politics.
30629-chicken-little-jane-on-the-big-joh:
Lily Munsell Ritchie writes Chicken Little Jane on the Big John, copyrighted in 1919 by the Britton Publishing Company of New York. An illustration shows a boy coming halfway across and holding out his hand. Eleven chapters open with Huz and Baby Jill in the pasture, harking back to Centerville, and Chicken Little paying a visit.

Later chapters add a cherry penance, guests arriving, a hunting party, pigs, and a party and picnic. Bread and polliwogs, supper at the captain's, and calico scenes follow. Ritchie writes a warm, funny children's tale of farm, river, and family, centered on a small heroine with a big heart.
611-prester-john:
John Buchan sets this South African adventure in the days before the Boer War's end. Young David Crawfurd, a Scots clerk, meets a black preacher named John Laputa on a Kirkcaple shore, then finds him again as leader of a rising meant to restore Prester John's empire. Treasure caves, drums at sunset, and a collar of kings mark the plot.

Buchan writes with boyish vigor and period views of race that modern readers will find dated. Captain Arcoll, a wily scout, guides Crawfurd through peril. The novel endures as a classic imperial adventure, brisk, vivid, and full of veld, gold, and faith.
6437-the-splendid-spur-being-memoirs-of-:
Arthur T. Quiller Couch, as Q, edits in modern English the memoirs of John Marvel, servant of Charles I in 1642 to 1643, dated 1897. Marvel, who jilted the Muse's gentle pipe for drum and trumpet, fears her revenge now he must write his adventures at home. On November 29, 1642, a clear, frosty day, the King, Prince of Wales newly recovered from measles, and Princes Rupert and Maurice march back from Reading.

Marvel, then a scholar of Trinity College, Oxford, begins at three o'clock, going for a fencing lesson to Mr. Rob. Drury, whose lodgings stand empty at Ship Street's corner by the Corn Market. Later, snoring like a dozen looms through a hut window over a stream draws him to peep before waking the sleeper. Quiller Couch writes a Civil War romance of a scholar turned soldier, with humour, danger, and a splendid spur to adventure.
8043-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: John's Gospel opens with a hymn to Christ as the eternal Word made flesh. From there it follows Jesus through signs and long discourses found nowhere else: water turned to wine, Nicodemus by night. The woman at the well, the raising of Lazarus, and the farewell teaching on the night before the cross. It closes with Thomas touching the risen Lord and confessing, my Lord and my God.

John is the most theological Gospel, concerned less with sequence than with who Jesus is. Its images of light, bread, shepherd, and vine have shaped Christian devotion. In the King James Version, its calm, profound prose makes it the Gospel many readers turn to first for prayer and meditation.
8270-the-world-english-bible-web-john:
John, in the World English Bible, opens as the King James version does, yet in modern prose. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and in him was life, the light of men, shining in darkness that has not overcome it. A note explains that the word for overcome can also mean comprehended, getting a grip on an enemy to defeat him. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the Gospel follows signs, discourses, and resurrection.

The modern version keeps John's theology luminous, from Nicodemus by night to Thomas's confession. Its notes help readers with difficult Greek words. For prayer and study, John here offers the fourth Gospel's depth in today's English, inviting slow reading of its claims about Word, light, and life.
8289-the-world-english-bible-web-1-john:
Whoever wrote 1 John cared less about argument than about assurance: how can believers know they belong to God? His answers are simple and repeated like a refrain. God is light, God is love, and those who know him keep his commands and love their brothers and sisters. Claims to faith without love are empty, he insists, and love without truth is blind.

Warnings against false teachers and against loving the world run through the letter, alongside comfort for readers who doubt themselves. Its short sentences and plain words make it one of the easiest New Testament books to read, and one of the hardest to live up to. The letter ends with a final guard: keep away from idols.
8831-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Weymouth's John, third edition 1913, begins where no other gospel begins: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him, and in him was life, the light of men, shining in darkness the darkness has not overpowered. John the witness comes to testify to the light, so that all might believe through him, though he himself is not the light.

From that prologue, Weymouth's plain English carries John's signs, discourses, and farewell teachings toward the Passion and resurrection appearances. The gospel's high theology and intimate scenes, Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, Lazarus, sit side by side in modern speech. Readers who find King James John difficult will gain a clear path into its argument, while students can compare Weymouth's renderings with more literal versions.
8850-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
The first letter of John, in Weymouth's modern speech, opens with testimony: that which was from the beginning. Which the writers have listened to, seen with their own eyes. Handled with their hands concerning the Word of Life. The Life was manifested, they declare, and they announce what they have seen and heard so that readers may share fellowship with them. That fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. They write so that joy may be complete.

The letter that follows turns on light and darkness, love and hate, truth and deceit, and the test that those born of God love one another. Weymouth's plain English keeps the letter's repetitions musical rather than confusing. Readers get the New Testament's great meditation on love as evidence of faith, short enough to read in one sitting and deep enough to return to often.
8851-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
The Elder writes to the elect lady and her children in Weymouth's second letter of John, loving them truly. Do all who know the truth, for the truth lives in their hearts and will be with them for ever. Grace, mercy, and peace are wished from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love. It brings intense joy, the Elder says, to find some of her children living true Christian lives, obeying the command received from the Father.

That command, he stresses, is not new but from the beginning: love one another, and walk in truth while refusing deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh. The letter is only thirteen verses, and Weymouth's version keeps its household scale: a brief note of encouragement and warning to a small community.
8852-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
The Elder writes to his dear friend Gaius in Weymouth's third letter of John, with simple affection: truly I love you. He prays that Gaius may prosper in all respects and enjoy good health, just as his soul already prospers. It brings intense joy, he says, when brethren come bearing witness to Gaius's fidelity to truth, that he lives in obedience to it. No greater joy exists, the Elder adds, than hearing that his children live in truth.

Gaius's faithful behaviour toward brethren, even strangers, earns praise, and the brethren have testified to his love before the church. The letter then contrasts the hospitable with Diotrephes, who loves pre-eminence and refuses workers. Weymouth's version keeps this shortest New Testament note warm and personal. Readers get a glimpse of early Christian hospitality, and of how much a small church's health depended on welcome.
9570-reminiscent-poems-part-3-from-volum:
Part three of volume two of Whittier's works gathers his subjective and reminiscent poems, verses of memory and self. Memories opens the run, picturing a bright girl whose mind wakes like a flower in spring light. The Pumpkin, Forgiveness, My Psalm, and The Barefoot Boy follow, each tied to home, youth, or faith. Whittier writes as an old man looking back on a long life.

The poems blend farm scenes, family love, and Quaker trust, with a tone both tender and firm. Snow-Bound, his best-known fireside poem, belongs to this same vein of memory. A reader gets Whittier's inner life in verse, warm and plain, and a record of what one New England life held dear.
9578-poems-in-wartime-part-4-from-volume:
Part four of volume three of Whittier's works gathers his poems In War Time, written during the Civil War. The part opens with a dedication to Samuel and Harriet Sewall, then moves to Thy Will Be Done, A Word for the Hour, and a hymn on Luther's Ein Feste Burg. Pieces on Fremont, the watchers, and Englishmen follow. At Port Royal, Barbara Frietchie, and Astraea at the Capitol mark the war's course.

Later poems hail emancipation, from a Newburyport hymn to the proclamation's anniversary. Whittier, long an abolitionist, greets freedom with prayer and praise, not triumph alone. A reader gets Civil War verse of faith and hope, written as events broke, by a poet who had waited decades for this hour.
9581-personal-poems-i-part-1-from-volume:
Part one of Whittier's personal poems opens with a lament for Charles B. Storrs and lines on the death of S. Oliver Torrey. Leggett's Monument, Lucy Hooper, and a note to a friend with Woolman's Journal follow. Channing, Daniel Wheeler, and Fredrika Bremer earn salutes, with The Hill-Top and Elliott beside. Ichabod and The Lost Occasion mark political grief.

Later poems in the opening group praise Wordsworth, Kossuth, and an old schoolmaster, before turning to The Cross and William Forster. Whittier ties each name to a cause or a memory. A reader gets the first gallery of his personal verse, warm, plain, and full of friendship.
9582-personal-poems-ii-part-2-from-volum:
Part two of Whittier's personal poems gathers verse addressed to friends, heroes, and public men. The Cross opens, honoring Richard Dillingham, a young Quaker who died in a Nashville jail for aiding runaway slaves. Other poems salute Charles Sumner, Burns, Garibaldi, and Lydia Maria Child, with Brown of Ossawatomie among them. Each piece ties a person to a cause Whittier held dear.

Later poems mark Bryant's birthday, Thomas Starr King, and a welcome to Lowell, blending praise with memory. Whittier's tone stays warm, plain, and earnest throughout. A reader gets a gallery of Whittier's age in verse, and a sense of the friendships that fed his reform life.
9583-occasional-poems-part-3-from-volume:
Part three of Whittier's occasional poems gathers verse for days, places, and friends. Eva opens, drawn from Mrs. Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin, when Eva's fate moved firesides across America. A Lay of Old Time, A Song of Harvest, and Kenoza Lake follow, with hymns for church openings and a golden wedding at Longwood. Lexington, The Library, and Centennial Hymn mark public hours.

Later poems salute the Bartholdi Statue, greet friends, and bid godspeed to travelers. Whittier writes for the occasion with warmth and craft. A reader gets a varied set of public and private lyrics, where a poet lent his voice to his age's milestones.
9589-tales-and-sketches-part-3-from-volu:
Part three of Whittier's Tales and Sketches opens with The Little Iron Soldier, or what Aminadab Ivison dreamed about. Aminadab, a portly, easy man, wakes at one in the morning after a night of kicking and threshing in sleep. His wife scolds his restless night, and his dream tale unfolds. Passaconaway, The Opium Eater, and The Proselytes follow in the part.

Other sketches include David Matson, The Fish I Didn't Catch, and Yankee Gypsies, with Patucket Falls and The Lighting Up beside. Whittier mixes humor, legend, and moral point with ease. A reader gets a varied set of his prose tales, where dreams, Indians, and Yankee folk share one fireside.
9593-historical-papers-part-3-from-volum:
Part three of volume six of Whittier's works gathers his historical papers, essays on men and hours of the past. Daniel O'Connell opens, answering Henry Clay's 1839 Senate slur on the great Irish liberator. England under James II, The Border War of 1708, and The Great Ipswich Fright follow. The Boy Captives and Black Men in the Revolution and War of 1812 add American scenes.

Later papers treat the Scottish reformers, the Pilgrims of Plymouth, Governor Endicott, and John Winthrop. Whittier writes as a moral historian, praising freedom's friends. A reader gets compact, earnest history essays, rich in New England and Irish memory.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-and-uncle-john:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this third nieces volume in 1911. Uncle John takes Beth, Patsy, and a new protegee, crippled Myrtle Dean, on a motor tour through the American West. Major Gregory Doyle paces the sitting room in the opening chapter, sure something has happened to Patsy, beside a dog called Mumbles.

Their car, a wonder on wheels, speeds behind the chauffeur Wampus through Indian country and coyote-haunted nights. Chapters promise a real adventure at last: capture, a fiddler, an escape, and the romance of Dan'l. Horsemen hail the travellers with a bantering welcome to Hades on the road. Point Loma ends the route, after confessions and tales of woe have sorted every passenger's past.
caesar-commentaries-mcdevitte-bohn:
Julius Caesar wrote his own campaign reports in crisp third-person Latin. W. A. McDevitte's English translation covers the Gallic War and the Civil War. Caesar presents conquest as orderly, necessary, and brilliantly led.

The Gallic War's seven books trace campaigns across Gaul year by year. The Civil War books then follow his fight against Pompey and the Senate. Caesar's style is famous for clarity, speed, and cold control. Generations of students learned Latin from these pages. Read closely, they also show a master politician shaping his own legend in real time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-saint:
Ambrose Saint John, Oratorian born in 1815, died at Edgbaston, Birmingham, on 24 May 1875, son of Henry St. John of the Barons St. John of Bletsoe. Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, gave him his M.A. and his lifelong friendship with Newman. Curate to Henry Wilberforce at Walmer and East Farleigh, he joined Newman at Littlemore and entered the Church about a month before Newman's October 1845 conversion.

After Maryvale he accompanied Newman to Rome for priestly ordination, then began Birmingham mission work as Oratorians in 1847, moving to Edgbaston in 1852. There he laboured zealously in the Oratory and its famous school, a fine classical scholar and remarkable linguist in Oriental and European tongues. Overwork translating Fessler on infallibility during Newman's Gladstone discussion caused his death, and Newman's Apologia tribute endures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistles-of-s:
The Epistles of Saint John are three canonical books of the New Testament by the Apostle John. For the First Epistle the entry weighs authenticity, canonicity, integrity, author, time and place, and purpose, then turns briefly to the Second and Third. The First Epistle is short, a hundred and five verses in five chapters, and its lateness might suggest no trace in the Apostolic Fathers, yet traces exist.

Polycarp, writing to the Philippians about 110 to 117, says that whoever denies Jesus Christ come in the flesh is Antichrist, an evident echo of First John chapter four. Harnack deems that witness conclusive proof that the First Epistle, and therefore John's Gospel, were written toward the end of Trajan's reign. Polycarp names neither John nor quotes word for word, since the Fathers cited from memory. The phrase come in the flesh also appears in Barnabas about 130.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-sai:
The Gospel of Saint John is the last of the four canonical Gospels in the traditional order. Ancient copies sometimes placed it after or even before Matthew. It narrates the life of Jesus from his baptism to his Resurrection and manifestation among his disciples. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its contents, peculiarities, authorship, composition, text, genuineness, and importance.

The Gospel falls into a prologue on the Incarnation of the Eternal Word and a first part on the public life to the eve of the Passion. A second part covers the Passion and Resurrection, with a short epilogue on the unrecorded words and works. The author follows historical order with special care for exact time and connection, chronicling the opening ministry almost like a diary, with four successive time marks at the start.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ida-hahn-hahn:
Ida Hahn-Hahn was a countess, convert, and authoress, born in 1805 and dead in 1880. She descended from one of Mecklenburg's wealthiest and most illustrious noble families. But her father, the famous theatrical count, squandered huge sums on drama, reduced the family to straits, and had to be placed under a guardian. Her pious mother's influence likewise repelled her.

The sixteen-year-old girl, due to prepare for confirmation, received a particularly superficial religious upbringing by her own admission. Her general education was just as deficient, leaving gaps she later filled by reading. At twenty-one she married her cousin Friedrich von Hahn, hereditary marshal of Basedow, hence her double name. It was a marriage of convenience, and the entry follows her path from society life to conversion and authorship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-von-:
Johannes von Kuhn was a speculative theologian of the Catholic school at Tubingen, ranked with Staudenmaier as its foremost dogmatist. Born in Wurttemberg in 1806, he studied at Tubingen and was ordained in 1831. He taught New Testament exegesis at Giessen. He moved to Tubingen in 1837, took the chair of dogmatic teaching in 1839, and retired in 1882.

His early work explored the thought of Jacobi. It opposed the destructive tendencies of Strauss in an unfinished Life of Jesus of 1838. His life's work, the Catholic Dogmatics, appeared only in parts. They were an introduction, a treatise on the knowledge, attributes, and unity of God, and a volume on the Trinity. Though never completed, it showed a clear thinker of remarkable gifts for philosophical theology, and his essays in the Tubingen journal carried his influence through the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prester-john:
Prester John names a legendary Eastern priest-king. A fabled 1122 Rome trip by a Patriarch John of India, with a visit to Callistus II, cannot be the legend's source.  Prester John's first sound mention stands in Otto of Freising's Chronicle, dated 1145.

Otto's source was Hugo, Bishop of Gabala, sent by Raymond of Antioch in 1144 to Pope Eugene III to seek help for Jerusalem. At Viterbo Otto met the Syrian prelate, and there, before the pope, he learned of a John who ruled the Far East as both priest and king. He had with his people turned Nestorian. A few years earlier John had beaten the monarchs of Media and Persia in a three day battle ending in the taking of Ecbatana.  Later lore finds his germ in Jenghiz Khan, the Mongol conqueror who crushed Islam's power in Central Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cyrus-and:
Cyrus and John were martyrs of the Coptic Church. They earned the titles wonderworkers and silverless ones because they cured the sick for nothing. This entry draws mainly on the encomium by Sophronius of Jerusalem. Nothing is known of their birth or youth, and sources disagree over whether John came from Edessa or Alexandria.

Cyrus practised medicine at Alexandria and preached as he healed. Then he fled Diocletian's prefect to a coastal town in Egypt, where he took the monastic habit and lived as an ascetic. John, a high-ranking soldier, sought him out, and the two were later martyred together. Three Roman churches once bore their names, and their feast is 31 January.
doe-osti-2573396-instantaneous-waveform-: Catching grid voltage flickers in real time got its DOE tech, and this report covers the waveform meters. The pages detail the gadgets. The grid engineers get their eyes. The eyes were instant. The gadgets were detailed. The meters were waveform.
doe-osti-3023219-frameworks-algorithms-a: FASTMath got frameworked, and this DOE SciDAC institute covers scalable math. The pages detail the technology findings. The computing folks get their data. The technologies were scalable. The data were computing. The institute was SciDAC. The math were frameworks. The technologies were scalable.
doe-osti-3029711-frameworks-algorithms-a: Math researchers getting their scalable toolkit wrapped up got the DOE FASTMath finale, and this final covers the institute. The pages detail the results. The computing folks get their closeout. The finale was technical. The toolkit were scalable. The researchers were math.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CisnerosRogelio: FBI Name Search Request Form: the bureau's Form 422 routed through the Name Searching Unit and Special File Room - the Rogelio Cisneros request. The bureaucracy's paper trail, complete. A US government document from the archive. Readers will find it rewarding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeLoreanJohn_De: A Newsday article dated July 27, 1987 covers a deposition involving car maker John DeLorean and the aging of documents. The piece reports on sworn testimony about how old certain documents really were, a question that turned on tests and expert judgment. The surviving record gives the article's paper, date, and subject, but not its detailed findings, so it stands as a dated news report on that legal fight.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GeorgeJohn_Geor:
An Associated Press report describes an unlikely rescue at sea. The U.S. Coast Guard and two Cuban patrol boats cooperated to save seven Americans from a grounded boat off Cuba. The rescue happened on Christmas, with the two Cold War rivals working the same water for the same crew.

Enemy services rarely share a mission, which is why the wire carried the story. For a few hours, seamanship outranked politics off the Cuban coast. The report preserves that brief cooperation in spare wire-service form, a small human footnote to a hostile decade.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinoJohn_Mar:
An FBI memorandum from Miami, dated May 8, 1964, is captioned 'Lee Harvey Oswald — Internal Security — Cuba.' It refers back to a report by Special Agent James J. O'Connor, dated April 4, 1964. O'Connor's subject was John V. Martino of Miami Beach. Martino was an anti-Castro activist whose name runs through the exile politics of those years.

The memo is a link in a chain: one agent's report on an exile figure, folded into the Oswald file by another office. Such cross-references show how the bureau organized a case with thousands of names. A reader can follow the paper from Martino, to O'Connor, to the file where the bureau kept its Oswald material.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SparrowJohn_Spa: Harold Weisberg, one of the earliest critics of the Warren Commission, wrote a direct reply to John Sparrow. Sparrow had criticized the writing of Weisberg and of Mark Lane, another leading Warren Commission critic. Weisberg answers back and defends their work. The short piece captures the sharp public fights that broke out in the late 1960s between assassination researchers and their reviewers.
king-john:
King John, by William Shakespeare, opens as King John receives Chatillion, an envoy from France. Queen Elinor, Pembroke, Essex, and Salisbury enter with the King. Chatillion has come to speak for the King of France. John asks plainly what France would have with them now. Chatillion greets him, then questions his right to rule England.

Chatillion calls John's majesty borrowed, and Elinor repeats the phrase in surprise. John tells his mother to be silent and hear the embassy. Philip of France, Chatillion says, claims England for Arthur Plantagenet. Arthur is son of John's dead brother Geoffrey, the speech explains. That claim, laid to the island and its lands, drives the scene.
occasional-poems-part-3-from-volume-iv-o:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote the poems gathered here. They form part three of volume four of his works. Whittier was a well known American poet and abolitionist. The contents list hymns, songs, and poems for public events. Titles include Eva, A Song of Harvest, and Kenoza Lake.

Many poems mark places, seasons, and civic moments in New England. Others honor friends, churches, and national anniversaries. Eva responds to the tale of Uncle Tom's Cabin. The hymns were sung at church openings and school closings. Together they show Whittier as a public, moral voice. Several pieces were written for named days and public gatherings.
personal-poems-i-part-1-from-volume-iv-o: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Personal Poems I, the title page and contents of part 1 of volume 4 of Whittier's works, with no poems visible. The list begins with A Lament and poems to the memory of Charles B. Storrs and S. Oliver Torrey, then runs through Leggett's Monument, Chalkley Hall, tributes to Channing and Kossuth, and the celebrated Ichabod and The Lost Occasion.
personal-poems-ii-part-2-from-volume-iv-: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Personal Poems II, the title page, contents, and a poem heading, with no verse text visible. Part 2 of volume 4 of Whittier's works opens with The Cross and The Hero, then offers tributes to Rantoul, Charles Sumner, and Burns. Memorials of Joseph Sturge and Brown of Ossawatomie follow, and poems for Lydia Maria Child, Garibaldi, Bryant, and Bayard Taylor.
poems-in-wartime-part-4-from-volume-iii-:
John Greenleaf Whittier, the Quaker poet of Massachusetts, speaks in this volume as America's conscience during the Civil War. The contents gather his In War Time group, poems written as the conflict burned: To John C. Fremont, the Watchers, the Battle Autumn of 1862, and At Port Royal, alongside the famous Barbara Frietchie, the story of an old woman defying Confederate troops with a Union flag.

Whittier had been an abolitionist editor before he was a war poet, and the anti-slavery fire runs through the collection. A hymn for the celebration of emancipation, the Proclamation, and pieces on St. Helena Island, where freed people were building new lives. A dedication to his old friends Samuel and Harriet Sewall recalls that these lines stood at the front of the original volume. The poems read as a diary of the Union cause in verse.
prester-john:
John Buchan dedicated Prester John to Lionel Phillips in a poem of farewell to youth. Time, he writes, must capture the best of us. Travel and battle and gems and gold can no longer kindle the ancient rapture. Yet in Phillips, he thinks, the boy is not over. So he offers this medley of ways and wars. It comes from a fellow-lover of the fairest country under the stars.

The country is South Africa. The medley is Buchan's first great adventure novel. Its narrator is Davie Crawfurd, a Scots storekeeper's assistant. Contents promise the man on the Kirkcaple shore, where Davie first sees a strange preacher. Then come fortune, the winter veld, and Mr. Wardlaw's premonition. Behind them waits John Laputa, raising a rising under Prester John's banner. A fortune in gold waits too. Few thrillers have ever matched its pace.
reminiscent-poems-part-3-from-volume-ii-:
John Greenleaf Whittier grouped these poems as subjective and reminiscent, in a third part drawn from his works. The contents list opens with Memories and Raphael, then turns personal: To My Sister, My Thanks, My Namesake, and My Psalm. The Barefoot Boy, his famed poem of boyhood, stands among them.

The first poem, Memories, begins with a beautiful, happy girl, her step as light as summer air. Her mind unfolds leaf by leaf like a morning flower, and her heart wakes like a fine-toned lute at every breath of feeling. Forgiveness, Remembrance, A Memory, My Dream, and The Waiting complete a set steeped in family, loss, and faith.
tales-and-sketches-part-3-from-volume-v-:
Tales and Sketches by John Greenleaf Whittier collects the poet's prose, drawn here from the fifth volume of his works. The contents open with The Little Iron Soldier, or What Aminadab Ivison Dreamed About, and range across New England history, folklore, and factory life.

Passaconaway tells of the great Penacook sachem; The Opium Eater and The Proselytes follow; then come David Matson, The Fish I Didn't Catch, Yankee Gypsies, and The Training. Patucket Falls and First Day in Lowell bring in the mill towns, and Charms and Fairy Faith and Magicians and Witch Folk gather the old superstitions. The first tale opens at one in the morning. Aminadab Ivison starts up in bed. He has had a tried night of kicking and threshing. He wakes to tell his wife his dream.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-43-joh:
John in King James translation, starts with the Word, who was with God and was God in the beginning. All things were made by him, the first verses say, and without him nothing made was made.

In him was life, and that life was the light of men, shining in darkness the darkness did not grasp. A man sent from God, named John, came to bear witness to that light, though he was not the light himself. The true light, the text says, lights every man coming into the world. He was in the world he made, yet the world did not know him.
the-lady-of-fort-st-john: Mary Hartwell Catherwood published this novel of old Acadia in 1891. She had written The Romance of Dollard before it. She dedicated the book to two Acadians of the present day. Dr. John-George Bourinot of Ottawa and Dr. George Stewart of Quebec are they. Both were natives of Nova Scotia. Only the title page, dedication, and preface's first line are present here. The story itself does not appear. The preface asks how we can care for shadows when we may go back through the past itself.
the-splendid-spur-being-memoirs-of-the-a:
Arthur T. Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, presents the memoirs of John Marvel. Marvel served King Charles I in the civil war years 1642 and 1643. He wrote the memoirs himself. The editor has put them into modern English. A dedication letter to Edward Gwynne Eardley-Wilmot, dated from Torquay in August 1889, explains that under Jack Marvel's coat beats the heart of the author's friend.

An introductory note then untangles a curiosity of the time: three writers were using the popular signature Q, and none would surrender the letter. The public, Quiller-Couch says, had to decide which of them was Q to it, and readers of this 1897 edition meet the claimant whose historical adventure follows.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-john:
Book sixty-two in the World English Bible is the first letter of John. Its opening speaks of what existed from the beginning. The writer stresses what was heard, seen, and touched. That testimony concerns the Word of life. Eternal life, once with the Father, has now been revealed.

The letter announces a simple message: God is light. No darkness exists in him at all. Walking in darkness while claiming fellowship is called a lie. Walking in light brings fellowship and cleansing from sin. Claiming to have no sin, John warns, is self-deception. Readers receive a short, searching letter on honesty, light, and forgiveness.
the-world-english-bible-web-john:
John's Gospel, book forty-three in the World English Bible, begins with the Word. The Word was with God in the beginning, and was God. All things were made through him. Life in him becomes light for humanity. That light shines in darkness, which cannot overcome it. A footnote explains the Greek word can also mean comprehend.

John the baptizer then enters as a witness. He is not the light himself, the Gospel stresses. He testifies so that all might believe. The true light was coming into the world. Readers meet a Gospel unlike the other three. Theology and narrative intertwine from its first soaring lines.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
First John appears here in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech rendering, third edition, 1913. It is book 62 in his New Testament set. The letter opens with a claim to have seen and touched the Word of Life. That life, the writer says, was shown to the world and can now be shared.

The early verses give the core claim that God is light, with no darkness in him at all. Those who walk in the light share life with each other. Confessed sin, the letter adds, meets a faithful God who forgives. Weymouth's plain words keep the short letter easy to read aloud.

Second John is book 63 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The writer calls himself the Elder and writes to a chosen lady and her children. He rejoices that some of her children live true lives. His one old command is that they love one another.

Love, he says, means living by God's commands. He warns that many who deny Christ in the flesh have gone out into the world. Such teachers should not be housed or greeted. The letter is short, and it ends with hope of a face to face talk. Weymouth keeps its brief charge in plain, warm words.

Third John, book 64 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech set, third edition, 1913, is a brief note from the Elder to his friend Gaius. The writer prays that Gaius may thrive and stay well in body as he does in soul. Visiting brothers have praised the man's faith and his open house.

Trouble comes from Diotrephes, who loves first place and blocks guests from the church. The Elder vows to face his conduct when he comes. By contrast, Demetrius wins praise from all. Weymouth gives the tiny letter in fresh, direct words. Readers see early church friendship, welcome, and pride in a few short verses.

John's Gospel is book 43 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The first line speaks of the Word, who was with God and was God. All things came to be through him, and life in him was light for men. That light shines in the dark, and the dark has not won.

John the witness then enters, sent to point men to the light. The Word came to his own world, yet his own people gave him no welcome. Those who did trust gained the right to be God's children. Weymouth's clear opening lines keep the deep thought easy to grasp.
